resources.string: Tap \"Start protection\" to block dangerous sites and ads in every app, on any network. The first time, Android asks whether the app may set up a VPN connection. It is used only on the phone.
Dangerous sites and ads are blocked in every app.

Blocking of dangerous addresses isn\'t active. The app downloads the lists directly from their publishers when the phone is online. Until then, only names are blocked.

Nothing has been blocked since protection started.
This list stays on the phone and is cleared each time protection starts or stops.

Without Android\'s VPN permission, the app can\'t see DNS lookups, so it can\'t block anything. The permission is used only on the phone, and there is no Cocode server. Lookups that aren\'t blocked go to the network\'s own DNS server, as before. Tap \"Try again\" if you want to give permission now.

The phone is no longer protected: DNS lookups aren\'t filtered, so dangerous sites and ads aren\'t blocked. Android stopped protection, for example because another VPN app took over or the VPN was turned off in Android\'s settings. Tap \"Start again\" in the app to start protection again.

The phone is not protected: DNS lookups aren\'t filtered, so dangerous sites and ads aren\'t blocked. The cause is Android\'s \"Block connections without VPN\" setting. With it on, Android lets traffic through only a VPN, and the app\'s VPN connection takes only DNS lookups and connections to known dangerous addresses. So the phone can\'t reach the internet at all. Turn the setting off in Android\'s VPN settings, then tap \"Start again\" in the app.
The phone is no longer protected: DNS lookups aren\'t filtered, so dangerous sites and ads aren\'t blocked. Something went wrong. Tap \"Start again\" in the app to try to start protection again.
Android keeps protection on, so you can\'t stop it here in the app. To stop it, turn off \"Always-on VPN\" in Android\'s VPN settings. Tap \"Open VPN settings\" to get there.
Protection can\'t run with Private DNS

The phone is not protected: DNS lookups aren\'t filtered, so dangerous sites and ads aren\'t blocked. \"Private DNS\" is set to a specific server. With that setting the phone can\'t reach the internet at all while protection runs, so the app has stopped protection. Tap \"Open network settings\", find \"Private DNS\", and choose \"Off\" or \"Automatic\". Then tap \"Start again\" in the app.

The app can\'t tell you if protection stops, so you could be unprotected without knowing. Tap \"Open notification settings\" and turn on notifications for the app. Also make sure \"Alerts\" is turned on.
The app collects no information about you, and there is no account, tracking or ads. What the app remembers about blocks stays on the phone and is cleared the next time protection starts.

The blocking happens on the phone. There is no Cocode server and no VPN server. Lists of dangerous addresses are downloaded directly from their publishers, who can see your IP address, just as a website can when you visit it.

Only DNS lookups and connections to known dangerous addresses pass through the app. A DNS lookup is how the phone finds out where a site is. Lookups that aren\'t blocked go on to the network\'s own DNS server, as before. The app never touches the rest of your traffic.
The app is free of charge, and anyone can read its code. It is free software under the GPL-3.0 license.
The app asks for only two permissions: VPN and notifications. It has no access to your contacts, location or files.
Works with TalkBack and large text sizes.
One limit: apps that use their own encrypted DNS bypass the name filter, so some dangerous sites and ads can get through in them.

Guard for Android blocks dangerous sites, ads and connections to known dangerous addresses in every app on the phone, on any network. Before an app opens a site, the phone looks up where the site is. This is called a DNS lookup. If the site\'s name is on the app\'s list of dangerous sites and ads, the phone gets an empty answer and the site does not open. Connections to addresses on lists of known dangerous addresses are blocked.

Android calls the app a VPN because it uses Android\'s VPN feature. But it is not a VPN in the usual sense: there is no VPN server, and your traffic does not go through an extra server. The app makes a local tunnel, a connection that starts and ends inside the app, on the phone. Only DNS lookups and connections to known dangerous addresses enter it, so the app can block them. All other traffic goes out as before. That is why Android shows a key in the status bar, and why only one VPN app can run at a time. If you use another VPN app, you can\'t run it together with Guard for Android.

The app is free of charge and released under the GNU General Public License, version 3 or later (GPL-3.0). You may use, read, change and share it. You can find the code under \"See the source code on GitHub\" below.

The name list of dangerous sites and ads is the AdGuard DNS filter from AdGuard (GPL-3.0). It comes with the app.
The Spamhaus DROP and DROPv6 address lists come from The Spamhaus Project, and the app downloads them directly from there. © The Spamhaus Project SLU.
The Feodo Tracker address list comes from abuse.ch (CC0), and the app downloads it directly from there.
The app is built with AndroidX and Jetpack Compose (Apache-2.0).
